claims.text: Under sustained loading, progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC HEA multilayers is primarily governed by interactions between dislocations and nanoscale interfaces.
Compositional complexity and short-range order produce severe lattice distortions in FCC/BCC HEA multilayers.
Severe lattice distortions impede dislocation activity.
Severe lattice distortions spatially concentrate dislocation activity.
Lattice distortions modify the barrier effect of multilayer interfaces.
Modified interface barriers enhance localized dislocation pile-up.
Localized interface conditions facilitate thermally assisted dislocation climb.
Dislocation pile-up and climb drive creep in FCC/BCC HEA multilayers.
The starting multilayer has alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC HEA layers.
The as-deposited multilayer has coherent, intact interfaces.
The as-deposited multilayer has a uniformly low or minimal dislocation density.
A sub-recrystallization elevated temperature can activate dislocation glide and climb without altering the nanoscale multilayer architecture.
Under sustained loading, dislocations nucleate and travel until they encounter multilayer interfaces.
Severe lattice distortions at or near interfaces promote localized stress concentrations.
Interface pile-ups transition to dislocation climb under thermally activated conditions.
The proposed dislocation process accelerates creep in a spatially heterogeneous manner.
HEA multilayers will have a higher localized dislocation density at interfaces than conventional metallic multilayers.
HEA multilayers will have a higher creep rate than conventional metallic multilayers.
Regions exhibiting pronounced lattice distortion or short-range-order variation will preferentially exhibit dislocation climb and accelerated plastic flow.
Significant thermal exposure, thicker layers, phase transformation, coarsening, or excessive stress may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
